claims.text: The initial Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA has a complex mixture of phases in the as-cast or solutionized state.
In-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction can monitor phase-transformation trajectories during heat treatment in real time.
Real-time diffraction feedback permits processing parameters to be adjusted during heat treatment.
Modifying heating and cooling parameters in response to in-situ measurements can influence phase nucleation and growth kinetics.
In-situ XRD can track dynamic changes in phase nucleation and growth kinetics.
Real-time synchrotron XRD provides immediate information about evolving phase fractions and structural changes.
Corrective changes to the thermal profile can favor stabilization of desired phases.
Corrective changes to the thermal profile can suppress unfavorable phases.
Using in-situ synchrotron XRD feedback during thermal processing leads to more controlled phase evolution than processing without such feedback.
Using in-situ feedback produces a higher fraction of the desired phase assemblage.
In-situ feedback will produce a more refined microstructure than the baseline process.
Conventional heat treatment without real-time diffraction feedback results in less controlled phase evolution.
The effectiveness of the method may be limited by the resolution of the in-situ measurement.
Thermal gradients in larger samples may limit the effectiveness of feedback-based phase control.
Feedback-loop limitations during rapid phase transformations may limit the effectiveness of the method.

contradictions.description: The experiment initially describes the monitored and unmonitored samples as receiving an identical heat treatment, but then states that processing parameters in the monitored set will be adjusted. Once adjusted, the thermal treatments are no longer identical, so the comparison conflates monitoring/feedback with differences in the applied thermal profile.
